slides.title: How coffee loses its caffeine
slides.subtitle: Three methods, and one step they all share.

slides.title: It happens before roasting
slides.body: Decaf starts as green coffee: the raw, unroasted beans. The caffeine comes out first. The roasting comes after.

slides.title: Method one: water and a filter
slides.body: The beans soak in hot water. That water then passes through a carbon filter that catches the caffeine. The same water can be reused on the next batch.

slides.title: Method two: a solvent
slides.body: Many decaf coffees are made this way. A solvent, such as ethyl acetate, picks up the caffeine. It is then steamed or evaporated off the beans.

slides.title: Method three: carbon dioxide
slides.body: Moistened beans go into a pressurized vessel. Carbon dioxide draws out the caffeine and usually leaves most other compounds behind.

slides.title: Every decaf, in three moves
steps: Pull the caffeine out with water, a solvent or CO2.

slides.title: Same goal, three different routes
slides.body: Decaf is made on green beans, using water, a solvent or carbon dioxide.
